name: Pala Empire
summary: A Buddhist empire in Bengal and Bihar, patron of the great monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.

knownFor.label: Somapura Mahavihara
knownFor.note: Huge monastery, a World Heritage Site.

location.value: The Pala stronghold was Bengal and Bihar; at its height the empire reached across the Gangetic plain to the Vindhya range and possibly Goalpara in Assam.

terrain.value: The flat Ganges plain and the wide, wet Bengal delta.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: hot, with very heavy summer rains.

resources.value: Rich rice land, fish, cotton and rivers for transport.

disasters.value: Floods of the Ganges and Brahmaputra and cyclones near the coast.

urbanisation.value: Royal camp-capitals such as Pataliputra and Mudgagiri (Monghyr), and great monastery towns.

disease.value: Malaria, cholera and other diseases of the humid delta.

migration.value: Buddhist scholars and pilgrims came from Tibet, China and Southeast Asia to study.

economicBase.value: The navy had both merchant and defensive roles in the Bay of Bengal, and Tamralipta was a major city; the page does not mention rice.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea trade with Southeast Asia, including Srivijaya, and overland routes to Tibet and north India.

wealth.value: Wealthy enough to endow huge monasteries; the evidence comes mainly from inscriptions.

moneyAndTax.value: Few coins: cowrie shells were common money; land taxes recorded on copper-plate grants.

inequality.value: Kings, landholders and Brahmins above farmers; monasteries held large estates.

governmentType.value: A monarchy in which the king was the centre of all power and appointed prime ministers called Mahamantri.

keyRulers.value: Dharmapala (770–810 or 774–806 depending on the historian); Devapala (810–c. 850 or 806–845); Ramapala, the last strong ruler.

succession.value: Hereditary within the Pala family, often between brothers and cousins.

institutions.value: Royal grants of land recorded on copper plates; great monasteries.

stability.value: Lasted about four centuries, with a revival under Mahipala I and a rebellion of the Kaivartas in the 1000s.

eliteConflict.value: Not well recorded; vassal revolts weakened the empire.

armyAndTech.value: Elephants, cavalry, infantry and river war-boats.

majorWars.value: Dharmapala was first beaten by the Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja; the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva then defeated both; Nagabhata II took Kannauj and the Rashtrakuta emperor Govinda III intervened. The page does not use the word “tripartite”.

territoryChange.value: At its height under Dharmapala and Devapala it reached across northern India.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival of the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; famous for bronze and stone sculpture and manuscript painting.

scienceEducation.value: Great Buddhist universities: Nalanda, Vikramashila (founded by Dharmapala) and Odantapuri.

openness.value: Very open: monks and students from Tibet, China and Southeast Asia studied there; Atisha left Vikramashila for Tibet in 1040.

communicationTransport.value: Rivers were the main roads; boats carried people and goods across the delta.

religion.value: Buddhist patronage: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura Mahavihara; Nalanda reached its height under the Palas; Atisha preached in Tibet.

languageWriting.value: Sanskrit for inscriptions and learning; early Bengali appears in the Buddhist songs called the Charyapada.

artsArchitecture.value: The Somapura monastery at Paharpur (a World Heritage Site) and the Pala school of black stone and bronze sculpture.

socialStructure.value: Not recorded in detail; kings, Buddhist monks, Brahmins, farmers.

sharedIdentity.value: Buddhist kingship and loyalty to the Pala rulers, with strong regional identities in Bengal and Bihar.

dailyLife.value: Brick and thatch houses in villages; rice and fish were the main food.

neighbours.value: The Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas (rivals for Kannauj), Kamarupa (Assam), Tibet, and later the Cholas and Senas.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Vajrayana Buddhism to Tibet through scholars such as Atisha.

riseSignals.value: Founded about 750 with the election of Gopala by the chiefs of Gauda; reign 750–770 per the infobox.

peakPeriod.value: Under Dharmapala and Devapala in the early ninth century the empire was the leading power in northern India; Devapala is regarded as the most powerful Pala emperor.

declineSignals.value: Weak rulers, the Kaivarta revolt, a Chola raid (1020s) and the rise of the Sena dynasty in the 1100s.

outcome.value: Disestablished in 1161 (infobox) and replaced by the Sena dynasty.
